intro: Today's four pieces split cleanly into two lessons: on the technical side, more agent architecture (multi-agent orchestration) and more agent autonomy both carry costs that need justifying rather than assuming, and on the banking side, both the regulator's own numbers and a rigorous LLM-explainability study confirm that surface-level AI adoption is running well ahead of real understanding or real trust.

cards.title: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026
cards.bite: This is the emerging standard vocabulary for what can go wrong with AI agents specifically, as opposed to plain chatbots. The core distinction: an agent isn't just answering a question, it holds goals, credentials, tools, and memory, and can chain actions together over many steps without a human checking each one — so a single bad decision or manipulated instruction can compound across a whole task chain before anyone notices. Expect security teams to reference these categories by code name in procurement conversations.
cards.read_if: Read if you'll ever sit across from a customer's security or risk team; skip if you only need the one-line summary of 'agents need new security thinking.'
cards.key_takeaway: Agent-specific risk is a different animal from LLM chatbot risk because agents hold delegated authority over time and across steps; the framework's own framing is that it covers systems with "goals, credentials, tools, memory, and the autonomy to chain them together over many steps."

cards.title: OpenAI single-agent LLM architecture reduces computational overhead relative to multi-agent orchestration in a simulated mars rover decision-support benchmark
cards.bite: A controlled benchmark pitted a single AI agent against a team of specialized agents on a decision task where all the needed information already fit in one input. The specialist-team setup didn't produce better decisions — it just used substantially more compute and took longer to respond. The takeaway isn't 'multi-agent is bad,' it's that splitting an agent into multiple specialists is a cost you have to justify with the task's actual complexity, not a default upgrade.
cards.read_if: Read if you need a straight answer for 'should we architect this as multiple agents?'; skip if your customer's use case is already known to be complex and multi-step.
cards.key_takeaway: For short-context, tool-less, static decision tasks where all relevant information fits in a single input, the study's conclusion is that <cite index="70-6,70-7">multi-agent orchestration should be treated as a cost-bearing design choice rather than an assumed improvement, contributing a reproducible architecture-level benchmark for evaluating when LLM-based orchestration is worth its operational cost</cite>, since <cite index="38-1">the most reliable difference found was computational efficiency: the single-agent architecture required substantially lower latency and token usage than the prompt-defined multi-agent orchestration architecture</cite>.

cards.title: Research Note: AI in UK financial services
cards.bite: Surveying 118 UK banks, insurers, and market infrastructure firms, the regulator found adoption is broad but shallow: foundation models are only 17% of AI use cases, a mere 2% of automated decisions run fully autonomously, and just 34% of firms say they completely understand the AI systems they've already deployed. The gap between 'we've deployed it' and 'we understand it' is the actual risk here, not the underlying technology.
cards.read_if: Read if you sell into UK or EU-regulated financial firms and want real numbers instead of vendor talking points; skip if your accounts are purely US retail banks.
cards.key_takeaway: Adoption looks high but depth is shallow: foundation models make up 17% of use cases, only 2% of automated-decision use cases are fully autonomous, and just 34% of firms report 'complete understanding' of the AI systems they've deployed — the gap between adoption and comprehension is the real risk, not the technology itself.

cards.title: Communicating Credit Risk with Large Language Models: Evaluation of Explanations from Standard and Alternative Data-Based Models
cards.bite: Tested on real mortgage data with actual credit risk professionals, this study found that AI-generated plain-language explanations of credit decisions are only as good as the underlying evidence method feeding them (SHAP-style feature attribution vs. graph-based explainers vs. combined approaches) — swapping which language model narrates the explanation barely matters. Critically, credit professionals graded these explanations by stricter evidentiary standards, while non-experts were more easily persuaded by confident, clear writing regardless of whether it was actually well-supported.
cards.read_if: Read if you're pitching 'explainable AI' for credit decisioning to a risk or compliance audience; skip if your deal doesn't touch model explainability.
cards.key_takeaway: The binding constraint on explanation quality is the underlying evidence representation (SHAP vs. GNNExplainer vs. bimodal), not which LLM narrates it — and credit risk professionals judge these AI-generated narratives by stricter evidentiary standards than non-professionals do, who are swayed more by how clear the writing sounds.
